item.title: Kurama Fire Festival: Torches and Flame in the Mountains — Guide
item.description: The Kurama Fire Festival, held on the night of 22 October in the mountain village of Kurama north of Kyoto, is one of the most dramatic and primal festivals in the region. As night falls, watch-fires are lit along the narrow main street and villagers, from children to grown men, parade enormous flaming pine torches — some several metres long and weighing over 80 kilograms — up through the village to Yuki Shrine, shouting as they go.

item.title: Nagoya Festival: The Three Heroes Parade Through the City — Guide
item.description: The Nagoya Festival, held over a weekend in mid-October, is the city’s biggest annual celebration, and its heart is the Three Heroes procession: costumed riders portraying Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu — the three unifiers of Japan, all born in what is now Aichi — lead some 600 participants in samurai armour through the streets between Nagoya Station and Sakae. Around the parade swirl historic karakuri mechanical-puppet floats, flower cars, marching bands and neighbourhood dance troupes, and many of the city’s museums and gardens open free for the weekend.

item.title: Kawagoe Festival: A UNESCO-Listed October Float Procession — Guide
item.description: The Kawagoe Festival, held each October and designated a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, transforms Kawagoe’s historic Kurazukuri storehouse street into a stage for towering, elaborately carved floats (dashi), some dating back centuries and adorned with mechanical dolls, lanterns and tapestries. As floats pass one another in the narrow streets, musicians aboard sometimes engage in playful ‘hikkawase’ battles, competing to outplay each other’s traditional flute and drum music in a lively display of local pride.

item.title: Dotonbori Halloween Guide: What It's Really Like in Osaka
item.description: Around October 31, costumed crowds gather in and around Dotonbori for an informal Halloween street party — Osaka’s equivalent of Tokyo’s Shibuya scramble. It’s spontaneous and unofficial: there’s no organised event, no stage, no tickets — just thousands of people in costume filling the Ebisubashi bridge and Dotonbori canalside to see and be seen. It can be fun and photogenic, but it’s also extremely crowded and increasingly managed by police. Here’s an honest picture of what it’s actually like and how to do it sensibly — plus better alternatives.

item.title: Jidai Matsuri Guide: Kyoto's Festival of the Ages
item.description: Imagine over a thousand years of Japanese history marching past you in a single afternoon. That’s Jidai Matsuri, the “Festival of the Ages” — Kyoto’s grand historical-costume procession held every October 22. Some 2,000 participants in meticulously researched costumes representing every major era from the Heian period to the Meiji Restoration parade through the city in reverse chronological order, a living timeline of Japan’s emperors, samurai, nobles, and famous historical figures.

item.title: Naha Great Tug-of-War Guide: Dates, Giant Rope & Access
item.description: The Naha Great Tug-of-War (Naha Otsunahiki) is one of Okinawa’s most extraordinary spectacles — a centuries-old festival in which tens of thousands of people heave on a colossal rice-straw rope right down the middle of Naha’s main avenue. The rope is so enormous (around 200 m long and 40+ tonnes) that it holds a Guinness World Record, and pulling it is said to bring good fortune. Held over the October sports-day weekend, the festival also features parades, eisa and fireworks, drawing huge, joyful crowds.

item.title: Osaka in October 2026 Autumn Weather Guide Events
item.description: Osaka in October: Weather, Events & What to Do — The Ultimate Autumn Guide October is when Osaka finally exhales. After months of punishing summer humidity that can leave even the hardiest traveler wilting, the city transforms into something magical — crisp mornings, golden afternoon light, and a culinary scene that shifts into high gear with autumn harvests. If you’re researching Osaka in October weather events what to do, you’ve landed on the best possible month to experience Japan’s second city.
